title: Exact efficient simulation of noisy logical magic states using Clifford stabilizers
authors: Yugo Takada, Stephen D. Bartlett, Dominic J. Williamson
abstract: The preparation of high-fidelity logical magic states is a crucial subroutine for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). Predicting the performance of FTQC and developing improved protocols rely on numerical methods to classically simulate logical magic state preparation in the presence of noise. Clifford logic on Pauli-stabilizer codes with circuit-level Pauli errors can be efficiently simulated using Pauli-stabilizer formalism, but the non-Clifford operations required to prepare logical magic states render generic simulation inefficient. We introduce Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an exact and efficient algorithm based on updating a Clifford-stabilizer group to simulate noisy preparation protocols for a broad class of logical magic states used to implement non-Clifford gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy under circuit-level Pauli errors. Clifford-stabilizer simulation applies to a range of operations that commonly appear in preparation protocols for such logical magic states, including Pauli-stabilizer measurements, logical Clifford measurements, and transversal non-Clifford gates. Our algorithm for Clifford-stabilizer simulation maps a non-Clifford circuit with sampled circuit-level Pauli errors to a Clifford circuit that exactly reproduces its measurement outcome distribution, achieving time and space complexities polynomial in relevant protocol parameters. We perform exact simulation of magic state cultivation up to fault distance 7 by Clifford-stabilizer simulation. Our method provides a route to perform exact benchmarking of large-scale logical magic state preparation protocols required for useful FTQC.
summary: This paper presents Clifford-stabilizer simulation, a novel, efficient algorithm for classically simulating the noisy preparation of logical magic states crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation. By mapping complex non-Clifford noisy circuits onto equivalent Clifford circuits, the method allows for the exact benchmarking of large-scale quantum error correction protocols. This provides a vital tool for assessing the feasibility of useful FTQC.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing an exact and efficient classical simulation method to predict the performance of fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) by simulating noisy logical magic state preparation.
main_result: The authors introduce Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an efficient algorithm that exactly maps non-Clifford noisy circuits to equivalent Clifford circuits, enabling benchmarking of large-scale magic state preparation up to fault distance 7.
method: The method involves tracking the evolution of a Clifford-stabilizer group ($	ext{GC}$) to simulate noisy protocols, mapping non-Clifford operations to an equivalent Clifford circuit representation.
model_or_system: The context is quantum error correction codes (e.g., surface codes) used in FTQC, focusing on preparing logical magic states required for non-Clifford gates. The simulation incorporates circuit-level Pauli errors and Pauli-stabilizer codes.
key_observables: Measurement outcome distributions, logical error rates, and acceptance rates for magic state cultivation protocols.
important_parameters: Fault distance ($f=3, 5, 7$), circuit-level Pauli error rates, and the size of the stabilizer group.
main_assumptions: The simulation assumes a specific noise model (depolarizing channel) and utilizes a systematic approach to map non-Clifford dynamics onto a Clifford-stabilizer framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate gate-teleportation circuits for T-gate implementation and the structure of surface codes for various distances, while tables detail the cultivation protocols for $f=3, 5, 7$.
paper_structure: The paper builds conceptually by first defining the problem, introducing the Clifford-stabilizer group ($	ext{GC}$), establishing update rules, and finally applying the simulation framework to detailed protocols for magic state cultivation and error correction.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the development of efficient classical simulation techniques for complex, error-prone quantum circuits is a significant computational tool relevant to understanding resource scaling in quantum information.
